title: Gutenberg's Secret Project
summary: Johannes Gutenberg was a clever metalworker from the German city of Mainz who worked on a big secret for years. He borrowed huge amounts of money, made shiny mirrors for pilgrims, and got pulled into lawsuits. By 1454 his workshop was printing its first small pages, and the world was about to change.

sections.heading: A Boy from the House of Gutenberg
paragraphs: Imagine the city of Mainz around the year 1400. It sits on the banks of the Rhine, one of the busiest rivers in Europe. Boats carry wine, wood, cloth and grain up and down the water. Above the rooftops rise the towers of a huge cathedral, because Mainz is ruled by a powerful archbishop, one of the most important churchmen in the Holy Roman Empire. Somewhere in this bustling town, a baby boy named Johannes was born.

We do not know his birthday, or even his exact birth year. No birth record survives. Historians work backwards from later documents, such as one suggesting he had come of age by about 1420, and they usually say he was born around 1400, with estimates ranging from about 1394 to 1404. In 1900, Mainz threw a big 500th birthday party for him anyway, choosing 1400 as a nice round number. According to local tradition he was baptized at the church of Saint Christoph, near his family's house, and the city still celebrates him around 24 June, the feast day of Saint John, his name saint.

His father was Friele Gensfleisch zur Laden, a wealthy merchant from one of Mainz's patrician families. Patricians were the old, rich, important families who ran much of the city's business and government. His mother, Else Wirich, was Friele's second wife and the daughter of a shopkeeper. Johannes had an older brother, also named Friele, and a sister named Else.

Wait, why isn't he called Johannes Gensfleisch? In medieval Mainz, rich families were often known by the names of the houses they owned. Gensfleisch means goose flesh in old German, which is a funny name to carry around. The family owned a large house called the Hof zum Gutenberg, the Gutenberg courtyard, and around 1427 the name Gutenberg starts appearing in records for the family. So Johannes Gensfleisch became known to history as Johannes Gutenberg, after his home.

What did young Johannes learn? Here the records are frustratingly quiet. A student named Johannes de Altavilla appears in the register of the University of Erfurt around 1418 to 1420, and some historians think this might be him, because his family had connections to the nearby town of Eltville (Alta Villa in Latin). But nobody can prove it. If he did attend, he would have learned Latin, which would help explain how he later printed Latin books so skillfully.

We do know that he became an expert metalworker. Later documents show him teaching skills like polishing gems and making metal objects, and he was linked with the goldsmiths of Strasbourg. Some historians suggest that his family had connections to the archbishop's mint in Mainz, where coins were made by striking metal with carved steel tools called dies and punches. Whether or not young Johannes ever watched coin-makers at work, his later invention depended on exactly those skills: cutting tiny shapes in hard metal, and casting soft metal into precise, identical pieces.

Mainz in those years was not a peaceful place. The patrician families and the craft guilds, who represented ordinary tradesmen like bakers, weavers and smiths, argued fiercely about taxes and power. Around 1428, the Gensfleisch family and other patricians left Mainz in protest over the city council's tax demands. Johannes's father had already died around 1419. From about 1429 to 1434, we lose track of Johannes completely. When he appears again in the records, he is living in another city.

sections.heading: A New Life in Strasbourg
paragraphs: In 1434, Gutenberg pops up in Strasbourg, about 150 kilometers south of Mainz along the Rhine. Strasbourg was a free imperial city, which meant it governed itself under the emperor, and it was much bigger than Mainz. It had busy markets, skilled craftsmen and a cathedral whose tall spire was being finished in those very years.

Gutenberg lived in St. Arbogast, a spot just outside the city walls, near a monastery. He was not poor. Like many patricians, he received an annuity from the city of Mainz, which was a yearly payment from money his family had invested there. His older brother Friele even transferred his own annuity to Johannes in 1434. But Gutenberg's first appearance in Strasbourg's records is a dramatic one.

Mainz owed Gutenberg 310 guilders in unpaid annuity money. A guilder, or gulden, was a gold coin, and 310 of them was a large amount. In March 1434, when a clerk from the Mainz town government happened to be in Strasbourg, Gutenberg had him arrested and held until his debt was paid. The Strasbourg council asked for the man to be released, and he was let go after promising that Mainz would pay. It tells us something about Gutenberg: he was bold, he knew the law, and he did not give up on money he was owed.

He also appears in a court case of a different kind. Around 1436 or 1437, a Strasbourg woman named Ennelin zu der Iserin Türe said Gutenberg had promised to marry her and then not kept his word. We do not know how that case ended. During the hearings, Gutenberg insulted one of the witnesses, a man named Niklaus Schott, and, according to the records, was ordered to pay him damages for the insult. There is no record that Gutenberg ever married, and historians think he probably stayed single all his life.

Records from Strasbourg's tax and customs books list Gutenberg as a half-member, or associate, of the goldsmiths' guild. That did not make him a full master goldsmith, but it shows he worked closely with metalworkers. In 1444, a list made when Strasbourg prepared for war against bands of mercenary soldiers called the Armagnacs shows that he had a fortune of over 400 pounds in Strasbourg money and had to pay for half a horse for the city's defense. He also borrowed money: in 1442 he took a loan of 80 pounds from the church foundation of St. Thomas in Strasbourg.

sections.heading: Magic Mirrors for the Pilgrims of Aachen
paragraphs: To understand Gutenberg's first big business, we need to visit the city of Aachen, in western Germany. Aachen's cathedral holds famous relics, objects believed to be holy, including cloths said to be connected with Jesus and the Virgin Mary. Every seven years, from 1349 onward, the relics were shown to the public in a great festival. Tens of thousands of pilgrims poured into the city to see them.

The crowds were so huge that most pilgrims could not get near the relics. Many people believed that holy objects gave off a kind of invisible blessing, like rays of light. So pilgrims bought small badges with a little convex mirror set into them, and held them up high toward the relics as they were displayed from the cathedral galleries. They believed the mirror would capture some of the holy power, which they could then carry home pinned to their hats or cloaks.

Gutenberg saw a business opportunity. In 1438 he formed a partnership with Hans Riffe, an official from the nearby town of Lichtenau, to make these pilgrim mirrors in large numbers. Soon two more partners joined: Andreas Dritzehn, who had been learning skills like gem polishing from Gutenberg, and Andreas Heilmann, a Strasbourg citizen. Each partner paid money into the business, and Gutenberg taught them his methods.

The mirrors were made by casting. The badges were made from a metal alloy of lead and tin. An alloy is a mixture of metals melted together. Molten metal was poured into moulds, cooled, and then fitted with the little mirror pieces. To make money, the partners needed to make many identical badges quickly and cheaply. Does that sound familiar? Casting large numbers of identical metal objects from moulds was exactly the skill that would later be needed to make thousands of letters of type.

But the plan hit a problem. The partners believed the next Aachen pilgrimage would happen in 1439. It actually took place in 1440, a year later than they expected. The partners were left with stocks of mirrors, debts, and a whole extra year to wait. So Gutenberg made them a new offer. According to the court records, he agreed to teach them all his arts and skills, including a secret new project. In the old German of the documents, the work is called an afentur und kunst, an adventure and art.

What was the secret art? The partners paid Gutenberg for it, and they promised to keep it hidden. Then, around the end of 1438, Andreas Dritzehn fell ill and died. Suddenly the secret partnership found itself heading to court.

sections.heading: Clues in a Courtroom: The Lawsuit of 1439
paragraphs: After Andreas Dritzehn died, his brothers Jörg and Claus Dritzehn wanted his share of the business. They argued that Andreas had poured a lot of money into the partnership, and they demanded that Gutenberg either pay it back or take them in as partners in his place. Gutenberg refused, saying the contract did not allow it. In 1439 the brothers took him to court in Strasbourg.

For historians, this lawsuit is a treasure chest. Many witnesses were called to describe what they had seen and heard, and the court clerks wrote down their testimony. Statements from a number of these witnesses and a copy of the court's judgment survived for more than 400 years in Strasbourg's archives. Then, in 1870, during the Franco-Prussian War, the library holding the originals burned. Luckily, scholars had already copied the documents word for word, so we can still read what the witnesses said.

What did they say? Several witnesses talked about a press. A wood-turner named Conrad Saspach had built it. A press is a machine that squeezes things flat, usually with a large wooden screw turned by a bar. Witnesses also mentioned lead and other metals, and objects they called forms. A goldsmith named Hans Dünne told the court that Gutenberg had paid him about 100 guilders, a lot of money, for making things that belonged to printing. In the old Strasbourg dialect, the word was trucken, which is related to the modern German drucken, meaning to print.

There was also a scene that sounds like something out of a spy movie. According to the testimony, when Andreas Dritzehn was dying, Gutenberg sent his servant, Lorenz Beildeck, to Andreas's house with an urgent message. The press there held four pieces, and the servant was to open it and take the pieces apart, so that nobody could look inside and figure out how it worked. When people went to look afterwards, the pieces could not be found. Clearly Gutenberg wanted his secret kept safe at any cost.

So what exactly was the adventure and art? Here we must be careful. The Strasbourg documents never clearly describe printing books with movable type, and no printed page from Strasbourg in this period has ever been found. The International Gutenberg Society in Mainz points out that there is no evidence he had yet invented his printing method or printed a book in Strasbourg. But the clues are tantalizing: a specially built press, lead and other metals, forms, a goldsmith making parts for printing, and a business owner desperate to keep it secret. Most historians believe Strasbourg was where Gutenberg began experimenting with the ideas that became his printing system.

It is also possible that some of the work was about making the mirrors themselves, or that Gutenberg was working on more than one invention. Inventors often have several projects running at once. What matters most is that by 1439, Gutenberg was already thinking about presses, metal casting and secrecy, three ingredients of his later success.

sections.heading: The Missing Years and the Return to Mainz
paragraphs: After the lawsuit, Gutenberg stayed in Strasbourg for a few more years. He is listed there in 1444. Then he disappears again from the records. From 1444 to 1448, historians simply do not know where he was or what he was doing. Some historians point to a Frankfurt document from 1447 that seems to mention a Henne Genssfleisch von Menze, which may mean he was already back in or near Mainz. Henne was a common nickname for Johannes.

The first sure sign of his return comes in October 1448. On that day, Gutenberg borrowed 150 guilders in Mainz, with his relative Arnold Gelthus standing as guarantor, which meant Arnold promised to pay if Gutenberg could not. The loan carried interest of 5 percent a year. Gutenberg was back in his hometown, and he needed money.

Mainz was still a busy trading city on the Rhine, close to Frankfurt, which held one of the biggest trade fairs in Europe. Merchants from all over came to Frankfurt to buy and sell, including books. If you wanted to sell a lot of copies of something, Mainz was a very good place to start.

Gutenberg set up a workshop in a building known as the Hof zum Humbrecht, which later became known as the Schöfferhof, after the printer Peter Schoeffer. There he gathered tools, metals and workers. Around 1449 or 1450, he made a deal with a wealthy Mainz businessman named Johann Fust. Fust lent him 800 guilders to build equipment for his project. A few years later, around 1452 or 1453, Fust added another 800 guilders, this time as an investment in what the documents call the work of the books. That made Fust a partner in the business.

How much was 1,600 guilders? Around 1450, a good town house in Mainz could be bought for about 500 guilders. So Fust's money together could have bought three houses, with some left over. It was far more than an ordinary craftsman could hope to earn in many years of work. Fust was taking a big risk on an unproven idea, and he expected his money back with interest.

Fust was not the only important person to join. A young man named Peter Schoeffer, born around 1425 in the town of Gernsheim, came into the workshop. He had worked as a scribe and calligrapher in Paris, copying manuscripts by hand. His knowledge of beautiful lettering was exactly what Gutenberg needed to make printed letters that looked as fine as the best handwriting. Schoeffer probably played a major role in designing the typefaces. He would later marry Fust's daughter Christina and become one of the most important printers in Europe.

sections.heading: Why Inventing Printing Cost a Fortune
paragraphs: Why did Gutenberg need so much money? Because he was not building one machine. He was building a whole new industry from scratch, with no instruction book and nobody nearby to copy from, and he could not sell much until all of it worked.

First, he needed letters. Each letter of the alphabet had to be carved, in reverse, on the tip of a steel rod by a highly skilled metalworker. Then those carvings had to be used to make moulds, and the moulds used to cast many thousands of small metal letters. As we will see in Part 9, getting every letter to come out exactly the same height and shape took clever tools and a lot of trial and error. Every failed experiment burned up time, metal and money.

Second, he needed metal, lots of it. Lead and tin had to be bought from merchants, and a big printing job needed many thousands of pieces of type. He also needed tools, furnaces, fuel for melting, and the presses themselves, solid wooden machines built by carpenters.

Third, he needed something to print on. Good paper came mainly from Italy and had to be bought in large amounts. For his most splendid books, Gutenberg also used vellum, made from calfskin. A single copy of a big book printed on vellum needed the skins of many dozens of calves. Buying paper and vellum for a large print run meant spending a fortune before selling a single page.

Fourth, he needed people. Typesetters, pressmen, metalworkers and helpers had to be paid, even during months when nothing was ready to sell. Historians do not know exactly how many people worked for Gutenberg, but making a big book would have taken a sizable team working for years.

Fifth, he needed ink that would stick properly to metal. The water-based inks used for woodblocks in Asia and for woodcuts in Europe did not work well on metal type; they tended to bead up instead of spreading evenly. Gutenberg had to develop a new, oily ink, more like the oil paints that artists of his time were using. More experiments, more cost.

Put all of this together and you can see the problem. An inventor might spend years and thousands of guilders before earning very much at all. That is why Gutenberg needed investors like Fust, and why the partnership became so tense. Fust wanted results and profits. Gutenberg wanted perfection. Those two goals would eventually collide, as we will see in Part 10.

sections.heading: The First Printed Pages from Mainz
paragraphs: Gutenberg did not wait to finish a giant book before printing anything. Like a smart inventor testing a new idea, his workshop also printed smaller things that could be sold more quickly. These early prints are rare today, and many survive only as scraps, but they tell an exciting story.

His earliest type is known to experts as the DK type. The letters stand for Donatus and Kalender, two kinds of items printed with it. The Donatus was a short Latin grammar book, named after Aelius Donatus, a Roman teacher who lived in the 300s. For more than a thousand years, European schoolchildren learned Latin from his little textbook, the Ars minor. Because every Latin school needed copies, it was a perfect product: short, always in demand, and easy to sell. Gutenberg's workshop printed several editions of the Donatus, many on tough vellum because schoolbooks got heavy use.

Almost no complete copies survive, because schoolbooks were used until they fell apart. Instead, scholars have found fragments recycled as stiffening inside the bindings of other books. Some of these fragments turned up in bindings from places far away from Mainz, which suggests that Mainz-printed schoolbooks were already being traded over long distances.

Another early print is a fragment of a German poem about the Last Judgment, the end of the world in Christian belief, sometimes linked to a work called the Sibyllenbuch, or Book of the Sibyl. It may have been printed around 1452 or 1453, or perhaps a little earlier; experts are not sure. Only a small scrap survives. There is also a short printed pamphlet in German known as the Turkish Calendar, made for the year 1455, which urged Christian rulers to fight the Ottoman Turks, who had captured Constantinople in 1453.

Then came a printing job that shows exactly why printing was useful. In 1454, a man named Paulinus Chappe came to Mainz. He was raising money for the defense of the island of Cyprus against the Ottoman Turks, and the pope had authorized the sale of indulgences for this cause. In the Catholic Church at that time, an indulgence was a document granting relief from certain punishments for sins, and people could receive one by making a donation. Each indulgence was a form with blank spaces where the name of the buyer and the date could be written in by hand.

Chappe needed thousands of identical forms, fast. Writing them all by hand would have taken an army of scribes. So in late summer 1454 he made a deal with Gutenberg to print them. Mainz printers produced a version with 31 lines and another with 30 lines, in runs of several thousand. One surviving 31-line copy was filled out in Erfurt on 22 October 1454. That handwritten date is the earliest firm date we have for European printing with movable metal type.

The 31-line indulgence was printed in a small, neat type that appears in no other book. Experts think it may have been melted down when the campaign ended, perhaps so that nobody could print fake copies. A number of these printed forms survive today, many of them, like the Donatus fragments, rescued from inside old book bindings.

Notice what these first jobs have in common. A schoolbook that every student needs. A calendar pamphlet. Official forms needed by the thousand. None of them was glamorous, but they proved the system worked and could bring in money. Behind the scenes, Gutenberg was already preparing something far bigger. Remember, too, that Gutenberg did not invent printing itself. Chinese and Korean printers had been printing with woodblocks and movable type for centuries, as we saw in Parts 5 and 6. What Gutenberg was building was a European system for producing metal type in huge quantities, and it all depended on one small, brilliant tool.
Gutenberg's real genius was not one machine but a whole system, starting with a tiny mould that could cast letters perfectly every time.

deepDive: Almost everything we know about Gutenberg comes not from his own writing but from legal and financial records: loan agreements, tax lists and lawsuits. He never signed or dated a single printed item, and no letter or diary of his survives, which makes him one of history's most important but least documented inventors. Historians piece together his story like detectives, and they often disagree. The Strasbourg lawsuit of 1439 is a good example. Its testimony mentions a press built by Conrad Saspach, lead, forms, and goldsmith Hans Dünne's work on items for printing, but it never spells out what the secret art was. Many scholars think Gutenberg was already experimenting with cast type in Strasbourg; others suspect the work may have been closer to the mirror business or to printing images, with type coming later. Because the original documents burned in 1870, scholars rely on earlier transcriptions, which adds another layer of uncertainty. Dates are slippery too. Fust's loans appear as around 1450 and 1452 in some accounts and as 1449 and 1453 in others, because they are known mainly from the Helmasperger Notarial Instrument of November 1455, which records Fust's lawsuit; his total claim, including interest, came to a little over 2,000 guilders. Experts also debate which early fragments came from Gutenberg's own shop, since none name a printer; attributions rely on type designs, paper and the places where fragments turned up. The earliest absolutely fixed date for European printing is the handwritten 22 October 1454 on a Cyprus indulgence. Money comparisons are rough guides: prices, wages and coin values varied from city to city and year to year, so a statement such as a Mainz town house cost about 500 guilders helps us imagine scale but is not an exact exchange rate. Finally, historians stress that Gutenberg combined many existing technologies, including metal casting, punch-cutting, oil-based paints and screw presses, into a new system. That combination, not any single part, was his achievement.
funFact: In 1439 witnesses said Gutenberg sent his servant to take apart a mysterious press with four pieces so that nobody could discover its secret, and when people later went to look, the pieces could not be found.
